original_interpretation: Merchant photomask makers compete with chipmakers that produce photomasks for their own use (captive mask shops).
evidence_found: "The photomasks required for those designs are manufactured by independent merchant manufacturers like Photronics and by semiconductor and FPD manufacturers that produce photomasks for their own use (captive manufacturers)."; "We also compete with semiconductor and FPD manufacturers' captive photomask manufacturing operations" (Photronics 10-K FY ended 31 Oct 2025, Item 1 Business, Markets/Competition)
notes: Opened via web_extract (sec.gov blocks the browser). 10-K adds that captives occasionally sell to outside customers and that market share has recently been moving toward independents.

original_interpretation: The US Bureau of Industry and Security described GAAFET technology as key to scaling to 3 nanometer and below technology nodes.
evidence_found: "GAAFET technology approaches are key to scaling to 3 nanometer and below technology nodes. GAAFET technologies enable faster, energy efficient, and more radiation-tolerant integrated circuits..." (BIS press release, 12 Aug 2022, ECAD bullet)

original_interpretation: In August 2022 the US imposed export controls on electronic computer-aided design (ECAD/EDA) software specially designed for developing GAAFET integrated circuits, effective 15 August 2022.
evidence_found: "The four technologies covered by today's rule include ... Electronic Computer-Aided Design (ECAD) software specially designed for the development of integrated circuits with Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistor (GAAFET) structure"; "The effective date is August 15, 2022." (BIS press release, 12 Aug 2022)
notes: Instrument was an interim final rule implementing controls agreed at the Wassenaar Arrangement December 2021 plenary (multilateral), not a unilateral US measure.

original_interpretation: Semiconductor packaging protects the chip mechanically, thermally and environmentally, and enables inter-chip communication, power delivery, and a platform for test and system integration.
evidence_found: "Semiconductor packaging serves two general purposes. The first is to protect the chip mechanically, thermally, and environmentally. The second is to facilitate reliable inter-chip communication, deliver power, and provide a stable test and system integration platform." (NIST NAPMP Vision Paper, 20 Nov 2023, p. 2)

original_interpretation: NIST's CHIPS program states that miniaturization under Moore's Law alone can no longer improve the performance of microelectronics, which raises the importance of advanced packaging.
evidence_found: "The rate of miniaturization expressed by Moore's Law alone can no longer improve performance of microelectronic technologies." ... "Advanced packaging innovations are central to achieving these requisite continued performance improvements." (NIST NAPMP Vision Paper, p. 2)

original_interpretation: According to NIST (2023), the vast majority of advanced packaging manufacturing capacity is in Asia.
evidence_found: "In addition, the vast majority of advanced packaging manufacturing capacity currently resides in Asia.3" (NIST NAPMP Vision Paper, p. 2; endnote 3 = IPC 'North American Advanced Packaging Ecosystem Gap Assessment', Nov 2021)
notes: NIST's statement rests on an IPC industry report from November 2021, so the underlying data are 2021-vintage.

original_interpretation: Chiplets are small, partially functional chips that, when assembled close together at tight pitch, form a highly functional subsystem.
evidence_found: "Chiplets refer to small, partially functional, semiconductor chips that, when assembled at tight pitch and close to one another, result in a highly functional subsystem." (NIST NAPMP Vision Paper, p. 5); "Small companion dies connected with advanced packaging are often referred to as chiplets." (Intel Tech 101, 'What is a Package?')

original_interpretation: Semiconductor test equipment is used at wafer level, packaged-device level and system level, and its customers include IDMs, fabless companies, foundries and OSATs.
evidence_found: "The test systems we provide are used for wafer level, device package testing, and system level testing of semiconductor devices."; "Semiconductor Test products and services are sold to integrated device manufacturers ("IDMs") ..., "Fabless" companies ..., "Foundries" ... and semiconductor assembly and test providers ("OSATs")" (Teradyne 10-K FY2024, Item 1, Products)
notes: Describes Teradyne's own products and customers; the claim generalises to 'semiconductor test equipment', which is reasonable but rests on one vendor's filing.

original_interpretation: When products are built from multiple dies, each die must be exhaustively tested as 'known good die' because scrapping a finished multi-die package is very expensive.
evidence_found: "If devices are constructed from multiple die, it is critical that the failure rate of any die be extremely low since having to scrap the final SIP is extremely expensive. Thus these “known” good die must be exhaustively tested before they are integrated into the final package." (ITRS 2.0 2015, Test chapter, p. 4, sec. 2.1.1 Increasing device integration)

original_interpretation: ITRS (2015) estimated fab costs at about 70-80% of the total cost of producing a large SoC, far exceeding test cost.
evidence_found: "Specifically fab costs for leading-edge processes have increased to about 70-80% of the overall cost of producing a large-scale SOC device. It now costs far more to fab a device than to test it" (ITRS 2.0 2015, Test chapter, p. 12, Test Cost Focus Topic)
notes: 2015 roadmap estimate, method not disclosed; ITRS was discontinued after 2015 (succeeded by IRDS). Keep labelled as a 2015 view; no newer like-for-like figure was found.

original_interpretation: The Standard Test Data Format (STDF) was developed by Teradyne as a common format for semiconductor test result data, with per-lot, per-wafer, per-part and per-test records.
evidence_found: "Teradyne has developed a simple, flexible, portable data format to which existing data files and formats can be easily and economically converted. Called the Standard Test Data Format (STDF)" (STDF Spec V4, Introduction p. 1); record-type table: "1 Data collected on a per lot basis 10 Master Information Record (MIR) 20 Master Results Record (MRR)...", "2 Data collected per wafer 10 WIR 20 WRR 30 WCR", "5 ... per part basis 10 PIR 20 PRR", "10 Data collected per test ... 30 TSR", "15 ... per test execution 10 PTR" (p. 6-7)
notes: Source is a third-party-hosted copy (kanwoda.com) of Teradyne's spec; identical text appears in other public copies (e.g. Google Code archive). source_type 'other' is acceptable for the mirror; the original is a Teradyne company document.

original_interpretation: A manufacturing execution system (MES) orchestrates operations in a fab, tracking materials, processes and equipment status in real time.
evidence_found: "The MES orchestrates all operations in a fab or foundry. Think of it as the central nervous system of the manufacturing plant, tracking materials, processes, and equipment status in real-time." (PDF Solutions blog, 9 Jul 2025, 'Key Data Types in Wafer Manufacturing')
notes: Quote confirmed. Source is a vendor blog (tier 3); claim_type 'fact' is generous for a vendor's explanatory statement - closer to reported_claim, though the definition is uncontroversial.

original_interpretation: Modern fab process tools may carry 100-200 sensors whose readings feed fault detection and classification (FDC) systems.
evidence_found: "FDC data comes directly from the manufacturing equipment. Modern fabrication tools may have 100-200 different sensors monitoring parameters like temperature, pressure, gas flow, and valve positions." (PDF Solutions blog, 9 Jul 2025, 'Fault Detection and Classification (FDC)')
notes: Vendor statement with no method; correctly typed as estimate and stays low-confidence (tier 3).

original_interpretation: PCM (process control monitor) electrical test data is one of the few data types foundries typically share with fabless customers, while defect and metrology data are usually treated as sensitive internal information.
evidence_found: "Interestingly, PCM data is one of the few data types that foundries typically share with their fabless customers. Other data types like defects or metrology are often considered sensitive internal information or “dirty laundry” that foundries prefer not to disclose." (PDF Solutions blog, 9 Jul 2025, 'Process Control Monitor (PCM) Data')
notes: Source says it; but this is a single vendor's characterisation on a tier-3 blog, so claim_type should be reported_claim rather than fact. Needs corroboration from a foundry or customer source.

original_interpretation: Semiconductor manufacturing data retention requirements extend 5-15 years depending on customer and application.
evidence_found: "The semiconductor industry generates terabytes of data daily, with retention requirements extending 5-15 years depending on the customer and application." (PDF Solutions blog, 9 Jul 2025, 'The Scale of Semiconductor Data')
notes: Vendor statement with no method; tier 3.

original_interpretation: Siemens markets its semiconductor MES as covering both wafer fab and assembly/test with single-wafer traceability, full genealogy, WIP tracking, recipe/mask/tool management and wafer-map management from foundry to final test.
evidence_found: "Enable single-wafer traceability with full genealogy"; "real‑time WIP tracking"; "centralized recipe management for recipes, masks, and tools"; "Deliver die‑level visibility from foundry to final test via wafer map management"; meta description: "a global MES to keep pace with demanding change in wafer fab and assembly/test semiconductor operations" (Siemens Opcenter Execution Semiconductor product page)
notes: Marketing page; correctly typed reported_claim. Browser hit a bot check; page text read via web_extract and a plain HTTP fetch of the same URL.

original_interpretation: Semiconductor production is commonly divided into three segments: design, manufacturing (wafer fabrication), and assembly, testing and packaging (ATP).
evidence_found: "Semiconductor production includes three segments: (1) design, (2) manufacturing, and (3) assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP)." (CSET Jan 2021, Executive Summary p. 3); "Three broad steps are involved in the production of semiconductors: (1) design; (2) manufacturing; and (3) assembly, testing, and packaging." (GAO-22-105923, Background, printed p. 3)
notes: GAO passage is on printed page 3 (PDF page 7), not p. 4 as recorded.

original_interpretation: 300 mm diameter wafers accounted for 99.7 percent of world fab capacity capable of manufacturing chips at 45 nm nodes or below.
evidence_found: "Wafer producers headquartered in Japan, Taiwan, Germany, and South Korea make state-of-the-art 300 mm diameter wafers, which are used for 99.7 percent of the world's fab capacity capable of manufacturing chips at ≤45 nm nodes.234" (CSET, p. 57; fn 234 = SEMI 'World Fab Forecast', November 2020 edition)
notes: Period can be tightened: the figure comes from SEMI World Fab Forecast (Nov 2020 edition), i.e. 2020-vintage capacity data. Old, but the share of <=45nm capacity on 300mm is structurally near 100%, so it is not materially outdated.

original_interpretation: CSET (2021) found that one Dutch firm, ASML, exclusively produces EUV scanners.
evidence_found: "One Dutch firm, ASML, exclusively produces EUV scanners, the most advanced photolithography equipment." (CSET, p. 32)
notes: Attributed 2021 finding; still consistent with GAO-22-105923 p. 6 ("one Netherlands-based company is the only global supplier for specialized lithography equipment needed to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors").

original_interpretation: CSET (2021) described the EDA software market as about USD 6.8 billion and dominated by Synopsys, Cadence and Mentor Graphics.
evidence_found: CSET p. 49, Table 17 "2019 EDA and core IP market": "EDA software $6.8 billion Synopsis (U.S.), Cadence (U.S.), Mentor Graphics (U.S./Germany), Ansys (U.S.), Silvaco (U.S.), PDF Solutions (U.S.) ..."; fn 189: the $6.8bn "includes four segments ... CAE ...; PCB and MCM; ... chip physical design and verification; and services" (source: ESD Alliance Q4 2019); fn 192: Synopsys 36.5%, Cadence 24.7%, Mentor 15.3%, Ansys 12.9%.
correction: The US$6.8bn is a 2019 figure. On the same definition (ESD Alliance EDMD: CAE + IC physical design & verification + PCB/MCM + services, excluding semiconductor IP), the four 2025 quarterly releases sum to about US$13.35bn for CY2025 (new superseding claim). Including semiconductor IP, CY2025 ESD revenue was about US$21.2bn.
notes: Attribution to CSET is accurate but the metric period is CY2019 (not 'year not stated'), and the top-firm list also names Ansys (12.9%), now part of Synopsys. Mentor Graphics is now Siemens EDA.

original_interpretation: CSET (2021) found that US firms are the exclusive providers of EDA software with the full capabilities needed to design leading-edge chips.
evidence_found: "U.S. firms are the exclusive providers of EDA software with the full-spectrum capabilities needed by engineers at fabless firms and IDMs to design leading-edge chips.192" (CSET, p. 50)
notes: Attributed 2021 finding. CSET counts Mentor Graphics (owned by Germany's Siemens since 2017) as U.S./Germany, so 'U.S. firms' includes a German-owned U.S. subsidiary.

original_interpretation: Experts consulted by GAO said semiconductor companies are hesitant to share information with each other, making actual demand for semiconductors difficult to determine.
evidence_found: "Two experts also noted that the federal government could bring industry together to create a clearer demand signal. One of these experts pointed out that companies are hesitant to share information with each other and thus the actual demand for semiconductors is difficult to determine." (GAO-22-105923, printed p. 17)
correction: It was one expert, not 'experts': "One of these experts pointed out that companies are hesitant to share information..."
notes: Location is printed page 17 (PDF page 21), not p. 14. Correctly typed as expert opinion, not a GAO finding.

original_interpretation: Experts consulted by GAO recommended a voluntary data-sharing mechanism improving visibility into second- to fourth-tier suppliers, without requiring disclosure of proprietary information.
evidence_found: "several experts said that the federal government should create and support a voluntary and timely data-sharing mechanism for firms that improves visibility into second, third and fourth tier suppliers throughout the semiconductor supply chain. However, some experts indicated that ... it would be challenging to implement."; "Some experts stated that the federal government should not require companies to disclose proprietary information when the government is collecting and mapping supply chain data." (GAO-22-105923, printed p. 14)
correction: Two separate expert views joined into one: 'several experts' backed a voluntary data-sharing mechanism for 2nd-4th tier visibility (some said it would be hard to implement), and 'some experts' said the government should not require disclosure of proprietary information when mapping supply chains.
notes: Both statements are on the page, but they come from different subsets of experts.

original_interpretation: The US Commerce Department found that the median inventory of chips held by responding customers fell from 40 days in 2019 to less than five days during the 2021 shortage.
evidence_found: "More than 150 companies responded, including nearly all the major semiconductor producers and the major automakers."; "The median inventory of chips has fallen from 40 days in 2019 to less than five days. These inventories are even smaller in key industries." (Commerce Dept. blog, 25 Jan 2022, RFI key findings)
correction: The source does not say the inventory was 'held by responding customers'; it says only 'the median inventory of chips', and respondents included chip producers as well as users.
notes: Number and periods confirmed. Commerce's RFI was voluntary; metric population should be 'median chip inventory reported via the RFI (respondents included chip producers and automakers)'.

original_interpretation: In the 2021 shortage, legacy logic chips used in automobiles and medical devices faced the most acute shortages, and analog chips were in extremely high demand and short supply.
evidence_found: "Legacy logic chips used in automobiles, medical devices and other products are facing the most acute shortages."; "Analog chips used in power management, image sensors, radio frequency and other applications are in extremely high demand and short supply." (Commerce Dept. blog, 25 Jan 2022)

original_interpretation: The US DoD's DMEA accredits trusted suppliers in IC design, aggregation, brokering, mask manufacturing, foundry, post-processing, packaging/assembly and test.
evidence_found: "DMEA accredits suppliers in the areas of integrated circuit design, aggregation, broker, mask manufacturing, foundry, post processing, packaging/assembly and test services." (DMEA Trusted Supplier Program page)

original_interpretation: The DMEA Trusted Supplier Program aims to assure the integrity and confidentiality of integrated circuits during design and manufacturing, preventing tampering and unauthorized reverse engineering.
evidence_found: "DMEA is the program manager for the DoD Trusted Foundry program. The program provides a cost-effective means to assure the integrity and confidentiality of integrated circuits during design and manufacturing"; trusted sources will "Prevent intentional or unintentional modification or tampering of the ICs" and "Protect the ICs from unauthorized attempts at reverse engineering" (DMEA page)
notes: The page names the purpose as that of the DoD Trusted Foundry program (which DMEA manages, with accreditation of trusted suppliers as part of it); wording is close enough.

original_interpretation: Smaller chiplets typically have higher manufacturing yields than large monolithic chips because they are smaller and simpler.
evidence_found: "Finally, chiplets typically boast high yield rates because they are often smaller with simpler designs, they start with known good dies after pre-bond testing and they can rely on repair strategies for defective interconnects." (imec, 'Chiplets ... (part I)', 16 Jul 2024)
notes: imec gives two further reasons (known-good-die pre-bond testing, interconnect repair). The comparison with monolithic chips is implied by the article's context ('Fragmenting large monolithic system-on-chips').

original_interpretation: imec identifies standardization, thermal management of stacks, power delivery and known-good-die testing as key challenges for chiplet-based systems.
evidence_found: "Size is just one challenge. A substantial part of chiplet research is dedicated to making the interconnections smaller ... When stacking chiplets together, thermal issues and power delivery (tackled by novel architectures such as backside power delivery networks) become critical. Finally, further standardization efforts are needed to ensure compatibility and communication between different chiplets." (imec part I, 16 Jul 2024)
correction: Part I lists interconnect size/pitch, thermal issues and power delivery in stacks, and standardization. It does not list known-good-die testing as a challenge; it mentions known good dies as a reason chiplets have high yield.
notes: Recorded evidence was a paraphrase. Part I says testing strategies are covered in part II.

original_interpretation: imec reports research demonstrations of die-to-wafer hybrid bonding at pitches down to 2 µm and wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at 200 nm interconnect pitch.
evidence_found: "We are developing die-to-wafer hybrid bonding with pitches down to 2µm ..."; "2024 press release: Imec demonstrates die-to-wafer hybrid bonding with a Cu interconnect pad pitch of 2µm"; "2026 press release: Imec and EV Group demonstrate wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with 200nm interconnect pitch and record high overlay accuracy" (imec 3D integration page)
notes: W2W 200nm result is a 2026 joint imec/EV Group demonstration; the same page's body text still says W2W work is 'currently aiming at 500nm pitch', which is stale text. These are research demonstrations, not production.

original_interpretation: Infineon announced a 300 mm power gallium nitride (GaN) wafer technology, stating that 300 mm wafers fit 2.3 times as many chips as 200 mm wafers.
evidence_found: "Infineon Technologies AG has announced the development of the world's first 300-mm power gallium nitride (GaN) wafer technology."; "The bigger wafer diameter fits 2.3 times as many chips per wafer, said the manufacturer."; "succeeded in manufacturing 300-mm GaN wafers on an integrated pilot line in existing 300-mm silicon production in its power fab in Villach (Austria)" (IEEE PELS, 13 Sep 2024)
notes: Also checked Infineon's original release INFXX202409-142 (11 Sep 2024, infineon.com/press-release/2024/infxx202409-142): same wording ("fits 2.3 times as many chips per wafer"), so no new claim. 'World's first' is Infineon's own claim; correctly typed reported_claim. Announced as a pilot line, not volume production.

original_interpretation: The main technology transitions under way (gate-all-around transistors, backside power, High-NA EUV, hybrid bonding/3D stacking, HBM4 and larger interposers) each depend on a very small set of suppliers: a single EUV tool maker, a handful of leading-edge foundries, a few EDA vendors and the memory makers producing HBM.
evidence_found: Inference; no source. Checked against the named claims: CLM-0397 (CSET: ASML sole EUV maker, verified here), CSET EDA concentration (CLM-0415/0416), foundry GAA claims (CLM-0401/0403/0406, unverified), TSMC CoWoS/SoIC (CLM-0435/0437, unverified), and HBM makers (e.g. CLM-0792: SK hynix, Samsung, Micron).
correction: Supported for EUV, GAA/backside power, EDA and HBM. 'Each' is not evidenced for hybrid bonding/3D stacking and large interposers, where the cited claims name only TSMC and imec.
notes: Reasoning holds for High-NA EUV (one tool maker, ASML), GAA and backside power (a few leading-edge foundries), EDA (a few vendors) and HBM4 (three memory makers). For hybrid bonding/3D stacking and larger interposers the cited claims show only TSMC and imec. They do not show the supplier set (foundries, IDMs like Intel/Samsung, OSATs, bonding-tool makers) or how small it is. Several underlying claims were still unverified when this was checked.
